utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60/1-S, the Prosecutor versus Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As we planned, this afternoon we'll continue the proceedings by hearing the Court witnesses. I would like to reiterate that the purpose of the hearing of those witnesses is for the credibility purpose only and not that the Trial Chamber has any doubts about sufficient factual basis underlying the guilty plea. This afternoon we'll have three witnesses. The procedure is: I, as a Presiding Judge, will ask some questions to the witnesses first to start the ball rolling, then the Defence may ask some questions, and after that the Prosecution, and later the other two Judges may put some questions to this witness. The first witness is Mr. Deronjic. This Trial Chamber made an order to request his appearance as a witness, and we also have his counsel present in this courtroom to observe the proceedings. Sir, would you please identify yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Slobodan Cvijetic, and I'm the accused's first Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. As the usual practice in this Tribunal, the counsel of the witness may make some interventions on the legal issues concerning his client's right, but he has no right to make any interventions concerning with factual issues. Do you understand that, Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we have the witness, are there any matters the -- Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I do not receive -- I'm not receiving any interpretation and I'm not able to follow what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may sit down, please, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just to explain to the parties about the procedures of this hearing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one moment. I want to clarify on yesterday's transcript. When Mr. Londrovic was questioning Witness DA, I think it was, in the transcript page 43, line 19 he was asking about the SDS membership, and as far as I followed the transcript, it says "SDA" there. We confirmed with the Prosecution to see if their understanding was also that he -- Mr. Londrovic referred to the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, so I would just like you to check on that part of the record from yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much to bring this matter to our attention, but I think there's no judicial damage to your part. Everybody understands that. I think then that -- could we have the first witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions. For the sake of the record, would you please be kind enough to state your name.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What is the date of the birth?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 6th of June, 1954.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What is your address before going to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I lived in Bratunac, Gavrilo Princip Street, number 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you somehow related to Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I'm not directly related to him, but my wife and Mr. Nikolic are related in a certain sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What was your position in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Up until the 11th of July, 1995, I was the chairman of the executive committee of the Bratunac SDS. On the 11th of July, 1995, I was appointed as a Civilian Commissioner for Srebrenica by an order -- by a decision from the Presidency of Republika Srpska. But I would like to clarify something and say that in some of the documents they say "civilian official." I don't think that's a correct definition. I think the correct term would be "Civilian Commissioner."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What's the difference between a commissioner and an official?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: A civilian commissioner is a post that's a well-known post in the former Yugoslavia and the Republika Srpska, in state spheres. It's a well-defined role. If necessary, I could provide you with other clarifications, but I haven't heard the term "civilian representative." This is not something that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, one word would be Serbian and the other Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I would like to draw your attention to the date, that is, the 13th of July, 1995. Was there a meeting in the night of that date in your office?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to correct a minor error. There wasn't an official meeting that was held. There was a meeting which turned into a discussion with regard to a certain subject. That would be a more precise way to describe this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Who were the participants to this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have on several occasions spoken about the event on the 13th in the SDS offices. With your permission, I would go into further details. Or would you like me simply to provide you with a list of the participants that I can remember?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I haven't understood your answer. Would you like me to go into greater detail, or would you like me just to name the participants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But first you have to name the participants.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I was present at the meeting, Miroslav Deronjic. At the time, I was a civilian commissioner. The meeting was also attended by Ljubisa Beara. At the time, I wasn't aware of the post that he held. I think he was a colonel in the Army of Republika Srpska. I think he had that rank. Now, I know that he was involved in intelligence in the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army. In addition to the two of us, Ljubisav Simic participated, but only partly at the time. He was the chairman of the Bratunac Municipality. And as I stated in my statement, I think that at one moment in time Mr. Vasic was present too. At the time, he was the chief of the public security station in Zvornik, and Bratunac is in its region, it's within its region. And there are no other people I mentioned who participated at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Was Mr. Nikolic present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: As I said in my statement, I don't remember Mr. Nikolic being Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Who was calling this meeting? Who is presiding over this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would you allow me to provide you with more detailed explanations about the meeting? The meeting wasn't called. It wasn't an official meeting, in the sense that people had been officially called to it. There was no agenda. There were no subjects or items set on the agenda. The meeting followed an event that had already occurred. In the evening, about 8.00 in the evening, from the Bratunac Brigade command I spoke to Radovan Karadzic, the president of Republika Srpska, through a military line. We spoke about captured Muslims in the town of Bratunac. I attempted to tell him about the impressions I had about the situation that had developed after the arrival of many Muslim captives in Bratunac, and I wanted to ask for instructions as to how I should behave towards those captive Muslims. There were many reasons for which I wanted to talk to Mr. Karadzic about the presence of the imprisoned Muslims in Bratunac; above all, I wanted to talk about security matters. Most of these captives were held in facilities which were not appropriate, in civilian facilities, in schools, in secondary facilities, et cetera. At the time, Bratunac was a town in which there were no men, because most of the able-bodied men were at the front, and because of all those captive Muslims who were there, there was a certain danger. There could have been attempts to flee. Panic could have spread. There could have been attempts to take revenge. Later on in the evening, I obtained information according to which certain murders had taken place in the town itself. The situation was really alarming, dramatic, and this is why I decided to consult President Karadzic, in order to obtain instructions as to how I should behave towards the captive Muslims. The conversation took place about 8.00 in the evening, as far as I can remember, and the conversation was recorded. The Prosecution has a tape, a recording of the conversation. And I would like to point out that I have also mentioned this conversation in all of my statements, and I have provided the details about that conversation at a time when I wasn't aware of the fact that a conversation had been recorded. I don't remember everything from the conversation. I remember some of -- parts of the conversation, and I conveyed what I remember to the Prosecution. This also included instructions about how one should behave towards the captives. I remember that at one moment Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic told me that someone would come with instructions and that that person would take charge of the captive Muslims who were in the town of Bratunac at the time. I returned to the office after the conversation. That was after 8.00 p.m. I didn't know that someone would come. I wasn't told that this would happen either. There's a record of this conversation. This can be checked. I wasn't told that someone could come to see me with those instructions. I returned to the office, and actually I continued to follow what was happening in the town of Bratunac, and I was expecting that the fate of the captive persons would be resolved, that something would be decided. I was waiting to see how all of this would end. Naturally, I didn't exclude the possibility that someone might appear in my office. But I didn't concern myself with such assumptions, and I hadn't arranged for a meeting with anyone; neither was this possible, because no one told me who would be coming and I had no idea about when such a person might come. I didn't know whether he would come in the course to have night or on the following day; that was also a possibility. So from that point of view, I did not arrange for a meeting. I admit that one may have said that he should be appearing in my office, someone should be appearing in my office, because I did raise the problem of these captives. But when he appeared in my office, I wasn't greatly surprised. But when he appeared, I was somewhat surprised after all, because I didn't expect him to arrive, at least not at that time. This was quite late in the evening. So I did not arrange for a meeting with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. You mentioned "he" or "someone." Who is he? Who is someone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I was referring to Mr. Ljubisa Beara. And I said that I hadn't arranged a meeting with him and there was no possibility. It wasn't possible for me to arrange a meeting with someone whom I did not know. I didn't know when he would appear in Bratunac. I was in the office, and I was following the events, and I was waiting to receive instructions from Karadzic to see what the fate of those captives would be. And I hoped that the instructions that he conveyed to me would be followed, that they would be respected. So when he -- when I said that he entered the office, I was referring to Mr. Beara. And as I said, I was somewhat surprised at that time because I hadn't been informed that he would be appearing in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And you told us that you went to the Bratunac Brigade commander and you spoke to Mr. Karadzic through the military line before the meeting. With whose permission did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. Just to -- to correct the record. It says that he went to the Bratunac Brigade commander. I believe he testified he went to the Bratunac Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, my question is that, you know, who gave you permission to go there, to make a phone call to Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't had the opportunity to tell you that in the evening, on the 11th, following an order from Mr. Karadzic, I was under the obligation to report to the Bratunac Brigade command, and that's when he informed me that I had been appointed as the civilian commissioner for Srebrenica. On that occasion, I met a low-ranking officer, and I told him that I had received an order from President Karadzic instructing me to speak to him. In the course of that conversation, President Karadzic and I agreed that if it was necessary to get into -- to get in touch, to talk about certain confidential matters, in such a case it would be good for me to use a military line, which is safer. It's safer than ordinary telephone lines, such as the line I had in my office, for example. So I was able to enter the command. I had access, and I could ask them to connect me to President Karadzic, because they knew that I had already spoken to him from the command. But at the time that I was there, there were no high-ranking officers present. This is what I have already stated in my statements. I met -- I saw a low-ranking officer there, and he allowed me to speak to President Karadzic. His name is Milomir Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And why do you think that Mr. Karadzic asked you to report to the Bratunac Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that he asked me to submit a report, the report about the captive Muslims. That was something that I did on my own initiative. He said in the course of our first conversation on the 11th, in the evening, when he informed me that I had been appointed as the civilian commissioner, he said that if I had any issues to raise, if there were any matters that could be interesting and that I wanted to inform him of, matters which were confidential, he said that such information should be conveyed to him over a military line, that is to say, from the Bratunac Brigade command. There were no other possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll come back to that meeting. Were there any issues that you discussed that evening?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: At the meeting in the SDS office, when Mr. Beara appeared, we first of all started talking. It wasn't the usual type of discussion. We didn't just start with a meeting and we didn't follow items on an agenda. As I have already stated in my statement, that is the impression I had and I think that the others were also under this impression, I was under the impression that he was under the influence of alcohol. Naturally, it wasn't that he wasn't aware of what he was doing, but it was evident that he was under the influence. When he appeared in the office -- the SDS Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. office consists of two rooms. I didn't see him immediately when he entered the first room, but he then appeared at the door to my office. That's the first time I saw him in my life. And on the following day, I never saw him again. I knew nothing about him. He approached me. Someone in the first office must have told him that I was inside, because he had probably asked for me. I don't know anything about that, but he appeared at the door. He approached me, and at that time I was sitting there with Mr. Simic, and I said that I could remember Mr. Vasic. He approached me, he greeted me, and he said that he was Colonel Ljubisa Beara from the Main Staff. I think I remember him saying that. I'm not quite sure whether he was a colonel at the time, but as far as I can remember, he said he was a colonel. In any event, a series of details captured my attention, his appearance, his appearance in my office. I asked him to sit down. We said the usual things, got to know each other, congratulated each other about having taken Srebrenica. I think we offered him a drink, a coffee or something, but usually whenever someone would appear in the office we would offer that person a cup of coffee. All I can remember is that he asked for some kind of a drink. One moment I wasn't out, I asked the secretary, "What kind of drinks do we have?" And we offered him some vodka. That's all we had. I remember we poured out a glass or two of vodka. I think I had a glass of vodka with him and maybe Ljubisav Simic, but I'm not quite sure about Mr. Vasic. So that's what happened during the first four or five minutes. He introduced himself, said who he was, that sort of thing. And then the conversation took a slightly strange turn. In my opinion, he started speaking in a slightly disjointed way and said that he had established contact with those captives and that they should be killed. At first I thought it was strange for him to start discussing a subject in this manner. I took the opportunity to take Mr. Ljubisav Simic, the president of that Bratunac municipality, out of that office. I'd just like to say that President Simic -- Chairman Simic hadn't slept for two nights. He'd been away on a trip, he was fairly tired, and in my opinion he didn't need to listen to such things because I thought that this man who had appeared was speaking in a disjointed way about certain things. I asked Mr. Simic to leave the office. I said that I was travelling in the morning. He knew that I had an appointment with Mr. Karadzic and that I was to go to Pale on the 14th and that it would be good for him to go home to have a rest so he could appear at work on time in the morning, and if necessary, if I wasn't there, it would be good for the chairman of the municipality to be there, in order to deal with certain issues, if anything arose. I then returned to the office. In my statement, I said that I wasn't sure. Perhaps I took Ljubisav Simic home. It's possible, but still I don't believe that that is what happened, but I don't want to get involved in guesswork. I probably asked someone to take him home. I returned to the office then. I left the office on two other occasions, and I have mentioned the reasons for which I did so. At the time, there were many people in the office. They were entering and leaving, especially in the first office, which is where the secretary was. I could go into more details about the general atmosphere if this is of any interest, and then you will understand that for various reasons people would come to that office. There were various reasons for which they would come to the office and ask certain questions. One of the reasons for leaving was that -- one of the reasons for leaving my office was that I heard that a certain Lukic had arrived and was looking for Mr. Beara. And the secretary insisted that I leave, which I did, and then I asked who this person, Lukic, was and what was at stake. I then realised who the Lukic -- who this person Lukic was. I know there is a Lukic who's been accused by this Tribunal. It concerns the Strbci case, and this is the Lukic in question. He appeared and he was asking for Beara, he was looking for Beara. I asked the secretary not to ask him to come in, because he could wait for Mr. Beara somewhere else. I suggested that he go to the Fontana Hotel and that he wait for the person there. Then I returned to the office. I left that meeting on one other occasion, because one of the soldiers entered. I remember that there was a crowd. He insisted on entering the office in which Mr. Beara and I were present, and perhaps there were some other people in the office at that time. I went out to tell him that no one should come in, and I saw a soldier. He had a beard. I can remember that. It was someone whom I did not know. And I realised that that person was not from Bratunac. I even thought at one point that perhaps that was Lukic. Later I realised that in fact it was not Lukic. He was looking for Beara and he wanted to speak to Beara about something. I told him that he had to go to Fontana too and that he should wait there and that Beara and I would finish our conversation very soon. I returned to the office again, and I then told Mr. Beara the following: "Mr. Beara," I said, "I have instructions from President Karadzic. For a certain period of time, I spoke to Mr. Karadzic and I was given precise instructions as to how I should behave towards the prisoners." I told him that the order that I had received from President Karadzic was that those prisoners had to be transferred towards Bijeljina and Zvornik, and I remember that I said to Batkovici too. Why to Batkovici? Because when I spoke to President Karadzic over the phone, when he mentioned further to the south, to the warehouses, and said that the prisoners should be placed there, I realised that that was the military prison in Batkovici. He didn't actually say that, but that's the conclusion I came to. So I told Mr. Beara that I had received instructions and an order and that I had to inform him that the prisoners should be taken in the direction of Bijeljina and Zvornik and to Batkovici. He then said to me: "I have orders instructing these prisoners to be killed in Bratunac." These prisoners were to be killed in Bratunac. And he said he had received these orders from the top. I continued to insist on the fact that there should be no killings in Bratunac. I had many reasons to do so. I told him that I had received instructions from President Karadzic and I insisted on this and I said I was not going to allow any murders to be committed in Bratunac. I said that those people should be taken away in accordance with the instructions that I had received from the president. I can't say exactly how long that dialogue of ours lasted, how long our conversation lasted about his intentions and his intention to take those prisoners to Bijeljina. I think that we exchanged a few more opinions about that subject, but it was a fairly tense conversation, almost a conflict that broke out between us. At one moment, I realised that he had accepted this reluctantly. I said, "on the following day, I'm going to see Mr. Karadzic, and I will tell him everything that you have informed me of, and I would be grateful if you could respect those instructions." He then reluctantly accepted this. He said, "All right. I'll take those prisoners there," he said. I can't remember all the words he used, and I'm not quoting him exactly. I allow for the possibility that we exchanged a few more sentences in connection with the safety of the prisoners in Bratunac that night, because I had a lot of information which had arrived during the night and before the meeting that there was insufficient security for these men, that there had been acts of revenge, killings, and also attempts to escape. And to conclude, the meeting ended in the way I have described, and I think that this is what can be of interest to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are you sure that Mr. Nikolic was not present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, a similar question was asked of me by the Prosecutors. I told the Office of the Prosecutor, and I will repeat again now: The atmosphere in my office was very unusual. Had this been a regular meeting convened by me in an official manner, I would certainly have been able to say now whether he was present or not. But as the meaning took -- meeting took place in the atmosphere I have just briefly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. described, all I can say is that I do allow for the possibility that he was present in the office; however, I do not recall him being there. And that's certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: My last question: How often did you see Mr. Nikolic on the 13th or 14th July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, aside from this meeting and the possibility of his being there, I did not see him again on that day. On the 14th of July, I went to Pale early in the morning and did not have an opportunity of meeting Mr. Nikolic. I remained at Pale almost the whole day. I remember only one meeting, on the 17th, in the UNPROFOR camp. I think it was Mr. Nikolic who took me there, and I participated in the drawing up of a document there. I remember that well. And I am not sure that -- well, there was another meeting on the 12th in the Fontana Hotel at 10.00, where I was present but Mr. Momir Nikolic was not at that meeting, or at least I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I turn to the Defence counsel, Mr. Londrovic, if you have any questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Londrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel for Mr. Momir Nikolic, and I will put certain questions to you to which I hope you will reply. Mr. Deronjic, in reply to His Honour's question, you just said that you allow for the possibility that Mr. Momir Nikolic was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't remember him there. Can you explain to Their Honours on the basis of what you allow for the possibility of Mr. Nikolic being present in that office without your remembering his presence.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I understand your question, and I will try to explain. The atmosphere in the office was such that the entry of Mr. Beara, escorted by several soldiers, caused a certain amount of confusion in the office. I'm not sure whether when Mr. Beara entered the first room, the first office, Mr. Nikolic came in with him. I didn't pay attention to that because I was sitting in the office next door. When Mr. Beara entered my office, I focussed all my attention on him, and all my attention was directed toward him. This was the first time I had seen Mr. Beara in my life. This is probably why I focussed my whole attention entirely on him. Had Momir Nikolic entered, that would not have been anything unusual for me, so I may even have noticed it but forgotten it over time. I do allow for the possibility that Mr. Momir Nikolic was among the group of people who entered the first office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I am holding in my hand a transcript of your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, and in one part of that transcript you say, "But I think Colonel Beara said -- I've noticed something else. Just let me say that. Some soldiers were coming into the office. They arrived behind him. I saw that, but there was confusion. Do you understand? I noticed that they were coming in. I don't know who exactly. I assume they were people from his security." Is this correct that this is what you stated in your interviews with the Prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that when some soldiers entered, after Mr. Beara, you think that Mr. Nikolic might have been in that group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: When I was making that statement, I was simply saying what had happened, without special reference to particular people. Now I say it's possible that Momir Nikolic was one of that group, because that would not have been anything unusual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. Mr. Deronjic, is it correct that in your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor you said that on the 13th a large number of buses and trucks arrived in Bratunac with imprisoned Muslims from the direction of Konjevic Polje and that this happened in the afternoon and the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to His Honour's questions, you told us about the security for these prisoners. And I think you said it was poor.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had information that it was very poor and that a number of minors had been mobilised, as well as people above military age in order to guard them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, you said that these prisoners were guarded by the military police and the civilian police. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then went on to say that even younger and older people who were able to carry weapons were mobilised in order to keep the situation under control up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's also true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, is it correct that during the night of the 13th you received information that some buses with Muslim prisoners had left Bratunac in the direction of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that on two occasions I received information that buses were going in the opposite direction from those coming to Bratunac, in the evening, and that was one of the reasons I wanted to talk to Mr. Karadzic, because this appeared very confusing and I couldn't understand what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, as far as I can remember, you said that this was the first time you had seen Mr. Beara in your life, that night.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you saw him again on the following day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours in what kind of situation you met Mr. Beara again.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, in the morning - I can't remember exactly what time it was - somebody woke me up, because of course after these talks in the office on the 13th, I went home in the evening. Somebody woke me up in the morning to tell me that Mr. Beara - I am referring to Ljubisa Beara, who had been in my office - that he had gone off toward a company. This was a factory producing bricks and brick products in Bratunac, and it was on the outskirts of Bratunac. Somebody told me that he probably wanted to take some prisoners there or that he had already taken them there; I'm not sure which exactly. And remembering what we had talked about in the evening in my office, I realised that he did not wish to act in the way that we had agreed on in my office. So I got into my car and hurried to see what was going on. I didn't stop by the office. I used my own car to go to that company. And on a bridge coming out of Bratunac, I came across a car. I saw it was a military vehicle, and I recognised Mr. Beara inside. I stopped my car, they stopped, and I asked what was going on. I said, "What kind of brickworks -- what do you mean? Why are you taking prisoners there? Why do you intend to take prisoner there when yesterday we agreed that this was not according to our instructions?" He was very angry, very abrupt with me. He said he had seen some warehouses there where he wanted to keep people imprisoned. It was probably to calm me down. And I said that this was out of the question, that I was on my way to Pale, and that I would inform the president of this. He was very angry. He was very nervous. He got into his car and he said something to the effect that he was leaving Bratunac. This was my meeting with Mr. Beara on the morning of the 14th. I don't know the exact time. And after that, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, this brickworks, this was referred to as Ciglana in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we called it. And I have been trying to describe it for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, please correct me if I'm wrong, but is it correct Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that at the meeting that was held in the evening of the 13th in your office there was open discussion of killings of Muslim prisoners and that you opposed this vehemently?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic, I have to correct you and tell you again that this was not a meeting. I insist on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. During this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was open talk of killings of Muslim prisoners, this can be interpreted in various ways. I have said exactly what Mr. Beara said about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll reformulate my question. In this "conversation" that was conducted in your office, did Colonel Beara openly say to you that all the Muslim prisoners should be killed and that you opposed this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Except for the word "all." I'm not sure I heard him say "all." He did say that, and he said that he even had orders that prisoners should be killed, and I did oppose it. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, is it correct that you insisted that the Muslim prisoners should be transferred from Bratunac further south, towards the territory of Zvornik and Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely correct. I did say that, and I adhere by that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you said that you saw Mr. Beara that night for the first time in your life.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, you also said that later on you learned that he was a security officer in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. Although, I'm not sure what the precise title is. It's something to do with security, intelligence. I get these things mixed up sometimes. But I know it was that kind of job that he was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was his job. Mr. Deronjic, is it correct that you know Mr. Momir Nikolic from before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that Mr. Momir Nikolic was the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that fact, to the extent to which I know what that is, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that you had dealings with the army.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, is it correct that Mr. Momir Nikolic was familiar with Bratunac as a town, that he knew it very well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. When you say "the town," for the sake of Their Honours I have to say that this is a small town, of 3.000 inhabitants, with practically two streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A small town.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a small town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, is it correct that Mr. Momir Nikolic knew where your offices were from before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely true, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, isn't it logical that Colonel Beara, a security officer from the security administration of the Main Staff, should be escorted by the security officer of the Bratunac Brigade, arriving in your offices, especially bearing in mind the fact that you did not know Colonel Beara from before, that is, that Colonel Beara had no personal knowledge of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what your question is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, my question was: Is it logical that Colonel Beara, who was the security officer in the security administration of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, should arrive escorted by Mr. Nikolic, who was the security officer of the Bratunac Brigade in your office, especially bearing in mind and placing this in the context of the fact that Mr. Beara had never met you personally, in person, before that and if we put this in the context of the fact that Mr. Beara was not familiar with Bratunac, to the extent that Mr. Nikolic was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I agree that everything you have said is very logical, but I do have a comment to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Do you think only logical things happen in real life?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will not comment on your question. Thank you, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request the Court that we take a break at this point. I would like to discuss the matter further with -- and I also need a break. I'm sorry. I probably drank too much water at the previous hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, do you have any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a few, Mr. President. Questioned by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you have testified today that Mr. Karadzic told you he would be sending you someone regarding what to do with the Muslim prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. But I wish to mention that he didn't say he would send someone to me. Rather, he said he would be sending someone with instructions as to what to do with the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it your understanding on who this person would be providing instructions to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, the person that was supposed to come, I did not exclude the possibility that that person might come to see me and give me certain instructions that I might receive from Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you feel a person came pursuant to what Karadzic had told you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Beara's appearance seemed to indicate that, and I thought that he was coming on instructions from President Karadzic, as he told me about his instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you about instructions? Are you referring to Beara or Karadzic now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I mean Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Beara ever tell you anything that made you indicate that he was the man Karadzic was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I would not be able to draw this conclusion, or rather, I was unable to make a direct connection because President Karadzic's instructions were that the prisoners should be sent off in the direction of Zvornik or Bijeljina, as I understood him. And he started saying that the prisoners were to be killed right there. To be sure, at one point he said, "I have orders from the top." I don't know who he meant. He didn't name any names, but I thought the instructions might be coming either from the Main Staff or from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you had any discussions with Mr. Karadzic prior to this evening that would give you any indication on what Mr. Karadzic might want to do with potential Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a conversation with Mr. Karadzic. In my report, it says that I talked to Mr. Karadzic on the 8th or the 9th. I'm not sure exactly which of these two days. And in that conversation, I said exactly what President Karadzic told me, and I was able to draw certain conclusions from all this and even link this up with the appearance of this man and what was said to me at Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So can you tell us what President Karadzic said to you at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pale on the 8th or 9th that you were able to link up with the appearance of Mr. -- Or Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told the Office of the Prosecutor why I went to see President Karadzic on the 8th or the 9th at Pale, and I explained having a brief encounter with him in front of the presidency building. I said that I could quote one sentence he said and that was the principle of Western Slavonia, when he was talking about what would happen in Srebrenica. Before that, he said, "Miroslav, those people there must be killed." That was his previous sentence. And then he said, "Whatever you can, you have to kill." And then he added a sentence that I can quote, that I'm sure of, and that was, "The Western Slavonia principle." He asked me if I had understood this, and I said, "Yes, I understand you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand him to mean by "the Western Slavonia principle"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It's a well-known fact that in May, if I remember correctly, the Croatian army mounted an offensive in Western Slavonia and Western Slavonia fell into the hands of the Croatian army. This was an area that had previously been held by the Serbs. And this event drew a lot of attention from the leadership of Republika Srpska, and in several meetings we discussed this operation and the conclusions were that the Croatian army in their attack on that area, which was mostly inhabited by the Serbs, had expelled the entire population from the area and that during this expulsion a large number of civilians and, of course, soldiers had been killed, and I drew the conclusion -- I'm not saying that these are true facts. I'm just saying that's what was said. And these were our conclusions about that operation. And I understood President Karadzic's sentence in this context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what specifically did you think he meant the Western Slavonia principle had to do with potential Muslims from Srebrenica during this conversation on the 8th or 9th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Karadzic uttered this sentence, as I said to the Office of the Prosecutor, I had nothing to indicate whether Srebrenica would be taken by the military at all. President Karadzic did say it was a possibility, and I assumed it was a realistic possibility. But I could not envision what would ensue in the military sense, the behaviour of the Muslim army in the Srebrenica area was unknown to me. I could not know what they would do, whether they would fight, whether they would try to break through, to pull out, and I didn't even think about that because I didn't have anything that would indicate to me how the situation might develop. And that's what I said to President Karadzic when he asked me what we intended to do down there. But later on I thought about his sentence, and I assume what he meant was that when our army entered Srebrenica and when the Muslim army in Srebrenica was defeated, that they would start pulling out. And I concluded that he thought that we should kill everybody we could get our hands on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I hope you could concentrate on the subject matter of these proceedings. Of course, you have another opportunity to examine this witness in the later proceedings in other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I recall the testimony of -- of Mr. Nikolic was at one point he said, "We had all been speaking to our superiors about this," what they were going to do to the Muslims, and so this point of Mr. Deronjic and his superiors is designed to try to, among other things, to see if -- if that was true, because of the way the testimony came out, it's a little unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on this meeting of the 8th or 9th, did President Karadzic actually say, "Miroslav, they should be killed," referring to any potential Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this is something I have told the Prosecution about. I mentioned this sentence to the Prosecution. I'm not sure about every word, but "kill," I remember this word being used. He said, "All those who are down there, they should be killed. Kill all those you manage to kill." That's what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the conversation that you had with President Karadzic at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters the evening of the 13th, did you know that you could be intercepted when speaking on that line?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have a -- I don't have any clear ideas about intercepting conversations. I'm really a layman as far as these matters are concerned. And I couldn't even have assumed that this could be recorded. I assume that Karadzic could have made such an assumption because at one point he said, "Don't speak about this very much." I remember that. And either he or someone else, an intermediary, said, "If there is something else you think you should inform me about, it would be good to do so via military tele-print." I think that is what he said. And after that, I didn't think it was necessary for me to clarify anything else, and I didn't provide any further clarifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the president said to you in that conversation, when you were in the Bratunac Brigade, "Move the prisoners out of Bratunac," or something to that effect, what at that time did you believe his intentions were regarding those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that at that time I thought that they were supposed to go to Bratunac. That had been stated quite precisely. It's true that it was coded, but the code, at least to me it was quite comprehensible. They had to go from Bratunac, he said "down there," that means outside Bratunac, and he said that they should be held in warehouses. I assumed that this was a prison. I drew the conclusion that, given that there isn't a military prison in Bratunac and there weren't any barracks or military facilities in Bratunac or Zvornik either, I assumed that he was talking about Bijeljina, and I relayed these instructions to Mr. Beara. But as to his real intentions, it wasn't necessary for me to attempt to draw any conclusions. This hadn't been required of me. I could have certain suspicions. I could have drawn certain inferences. But I wouldn't want to speculate about what I thought was behind something that had been said, that one could read between the lines. I didn't think that I heard him say, "Don't kill them here or in some other place," I didn't hear any words to that effect, and I can't claim that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your meeting with Mr. Beara, what was your conclusions regarding President Karadzic's intentions regarding the fate of those Muslim prisoners? And I'm talking immediately after that night.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If Karadzic conveyed orders to Mr. Beara, then those intentions were quite clear to me, because he spoke about killing those people. I can't confirm this. I don't have any information which would demonstrate that Karadzic gave such orders to Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the meeting -- well, after the discussions you had at your offices that late night, the 13th, early morning hours of the 14th, did you tell Mr. Nikolic about that meeting or talk -- talk to him about what went on at that meeting, about Beara talking about killing prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: You're referring to Mr. Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I said that on the following day I hadn't seen Mr. Momir Nikolic. I can't remember when I saw him the next time. Right up until the 17th of April, when the atmosphere was quite different and we were compiling a document concerning the evacuation of the civilians from Potocari. On that occasion I didn't mention anything to him about my conversation with Mr. Beara. We didn't speak about that subject at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time have you spoken to -- at any time up until the time you were arrested have you spoken to Mr. Momir Nikolic about what Beara had said that night in your office?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: This is something that I can affirm before the Trial Chamber, and Mr. Nikolic is here too. After these events, I didn't speak to Mr. Nikolic about the events in Srebrenica. I knew that Mr. Nikolic was under investigation. I had such information. And from 1998, I've been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. summoned by the investigators from the Office of the Prosecution. I thought that it was his right to say what he had to say. I also said what I -- I also spoke about what I could remember. I never spoke to Momir about any events relating to Srebrenica. I think that during that period of time, from the end of the war until the time I was arrested, I think that I -- during that period, I only went to his home on one occasion and for different reasons, and that was the only time I was in his house. But we didn't speak about this matter on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say the first time you told the Office of the Prosecutor that Beara had actually spoken directly to you about killing Muslim prisoners was in your very recent interview prior to your guilty plea?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps I haven't fully understood the question, perhaps because of the interpretation. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the first time you told the Office of the Prosecutor that Beara had actually talked to you personally about killing Muslim prisoners was in your recent interviews just prior to the guilty plea?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I said in my last interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Questions from the Judges? Judge Vassylenko? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you testified that you know Momir Nikolic for a long time. Can you be more specific? Since what time do you know Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know a lot of people in Bratunac. I was born in Bratunac -- I was born in a village near Bratunac, and I have spent most of my life in Bratunac. This is also the case for Momir Nikolic. It's a small place. I didn't have any contact with Momir Nikolic up until the war. We knew each other, but I can't remember ever having sat down with him somewhere, I can't remember having spoken to him about something important. Perhaps that doesn't appear logical, but Mr. Momir Nikolic could confirm this. What would the reason be for this? I had another circle of friends, a different perspective on life, and I assume that was the reason. But I did know his family; I knew his father. I think I knew his father better than Momir, because I would often go to an old-age pensioners' club which was visited by his father. We would sometimes play chess together, and this is a person about whom I have an excellent opinion. I got to know Momir better during the war, in the period during which the SDS was established, I didn't know Momir. Momir wasn't an SDS member - I checked this - and he wasn't involved in the activities that concerned the establishment of the SDS in Bratunac, and he wasn't involved in an organ of that party either At the beginning of the war, I got to know him during a period when the JNA was present in Bratunac, and that is the period for which I've been accused before this Tribunal. It concerns the period beginning at the end of April and continues up to the end of May. During that period, I met Momir Nikolic a few times, but this wasn't a relationship of a subordinate to a superior, because the army was present in Bratunac and Momir Nikolic would establish contact with them and he was present at some meetings of the Crisis Staff during that period. I remember him from that time. After those events, Momir Nikolic, as far as I know, because of a conflict with extremists in Bratunac, left Bratunac after an unfortunate incident, after a lot of soldiers of ours had been killed. He had problems with extremists and he left Bratunac. I didn't see him for a long time, and as far as I can remember - I'm not claiming this is correct - but he returned to Bratunac, as far as I can remember, at the beginning of autumn 1992. It was in the autumn. I can remember that he was working in the army. He had some other post there. My attitude towards the army is well known. I could speak about that for days. I would very rarely go to the command. I did meet Momir Nikolic quite frequently, but we never spoke about this officially and I didn't think that there was anything that I had to inform him of. I know his family well. I know his sons; I know his wife. We would often meet in formal situations after the war, but in the pre-war period I don't remember ever having been together with him somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You were president of the Crisis Staff in Bratunac municipality; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You just stated that Momir Nikolic participated in some meetings of the Crisis Staff. What was his role in the Crisis Staff? Was he invited or he appeared at the meetings of the Crisis Staff ex officio?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I think that the war broke out when Mr. Momir Nikolic was involved in his duties in the Territorial Defence staff in Bratunac. I've explained this to the Prosecution. I had an intention after the Muslims left the municipal organs in Bratunac, my intention was to form a Territorial Defence staff by using the Serbs who had remained in that organ, a Territorial Defence staff in Bratunac. And to this effect, I held a meeting in the Territorial Defence staff. I can't remember whether Momir Nikolic attended the meeting. I assume that he did. We didn't manage to agree on transforming this municipal organ. When the army arrived, about the 20th of April in Bratunac, then things changed. That was still the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and it's a well-known fact - I hope it's something that Momir Nikolic is aware of too - the army introduced military administration at that time. Towards the end of April, we continued with our activities regarding the establishment of a Crisis Staff. At that time, I wasn't paying much attention to these military issues or to the organisation of the Territorial Defence. I realised that the commander of the town, Mr. -- Captain Reljic, was constantly in that staff. He had his office there, and he formed -- he had formed a Territorial Defence staff there. I don't know when he did this exactly, and I don't know when he appointed Momir Nikolic as the commander of that staff. In this capacity, Momir Nikolic attended several meetings to have Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: In the interviews, Jean-Rene Ruez, investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor in February of 1998, you stated that, "Momir Nikolic was surely involved in the operation of evacuation, security, and other different tasks." Can you please be more specific? What other different tasks? And what was the role of Momir Nikolic in this operation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that I had information that I had been provided with by someone. I've told the Prosecution about this. I heard information, according to which, in addition to other prominent officers and police officials in Potocari, at the time the evacuation of the civilian population was commencing, I had information according to which Momir Nikolic was present. I thought it was logical for him to be present there, because he had certain command responsibilities with respect to the military police. I didn't think it was odd that he should be present there. General Mladic was there too, high-ranking Republika Srpska army officers were there, and I didn't think it was particularly strange that Mr. Nikolic was there. I had that information. That is what I was referring to. I know that he participated in the transfer of the civilians because there was a task they had to carry out with the military police. They had to take charge of those people, put them on buses, and take them away in the direction of Kladanj in the territory under the control of the Muslim army. These are things I was aware of. I know that in such a situation - and this is information I was provided with too - I know that it was said that Momir Nikolic had something to do with providing security for the prisoners who had arrived in Bratunac on the 13th in the afternoon and had been provided with accommodation in various locations in Bratunac. I was informed that the military police was also providing security for those buses, and I assumed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that Momir Nikolic played a role in this too. If I mentioned certain other duties -- well, I assumed that he had other obligations, but I really never heard about what other precise tasks he might have had, but I mentioned that because in my opinion these weren't the only duties he had to perform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Argibay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, sir. I have one or go questions -- one or two questions. In that same statement or conversation, I mean between the investigator of the OTP, Jean-Rene Ruez that has been in the 12th of March 2001 with you, talking about how you could have connected with Colonel Beara or waiting for Beara to appear, the investigator told you that there was an easier option, that would be to summon Momir Nikolic and ask him to do the contact. And you answered - and this is what I want to ask you - "During those nights, you could much easier found Kissinger in Bratunac than Nikolic." So that had to do with the night of the 13th of July. Why was it so difficult to find Nikolic and why, then, you are not sure now if he was there at that meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it hasn't been correctly translated to me. I know exactly what I said. The interpretation I received was that it would be easier for me to find Nikolic there. I said it would probably have been easier for me to find Kissinger there in Bratunac that night. That's what I said. I said it would be easier to find Kissinger than Mr. Nikolic. Why did I say this? On several occasions, Mr. Ruez tried to establish a link between me and Mr. Nikolic. When he told me - and I think I even remember the way he said this; it was quite nervous and angry, as far as his tone is concerned - he said, "Couldn't you have summoned Mr. Nikolic to ask him how many prisoners there were who had arrived in that -- during that period in Bratunac?" I said I didn't go there and I didn't have that information. I was provided with various pieces of information, but I didn't go there. They were located at various sites. It was night, and I didn't go to see how many people there were there. And I told him how I would communicate with Mr. Nikolic. I said he wasn't in the office. In such circumstances, he would be in the field. I assumed he would use Motorolas to communicate with his superiors. I didn't have such a device. I couldn't phone him. I didn't know where he was. I didn't say all of these things. But since they kept mentioning Mr. Nikolic, I said that it would have been easier for me to meet Mr. Kissinger in Bratunac than Mr. Nikolic. I was nervous because they were assuming that it was very easy for me to find Mr. Nikolic in all that confusion, in all that chaos, and that there was some possibility for me to find Mr. Nikolic. That wasn't a possibility. And not a single officer from the Bratunac Brigade command and not a single officer from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska -- well, I didn't have any contact with any of the officers from these places. None of these officers ever entered my office to assign me a task, and I didn't have a way of communicating directly with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: But you told us that you were able to use the Bratunac Brigade command facilities on telephone communication, if you could use that to communicate with Karadzic. It was not easier to find a lower officer in the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I went to the Bratunac Brigade command on two occasions. The Bratunac Brigade command is at some distance from my office. I would have to drive there. Secondly, I only once saw a duty officer or such a low-ranking duty officer there. I'm not even sure whether I was aware of the fact that he was an officer in the Bratunac Brigade. I know that man, but I hadn't noticed that he was an officer in the Bratunac Brigade. If you now ask me to tell you the composition of the Bratunac Brigade, I can tell you under oath that this is not possible for me to do. He was such a low-ranking official that I didn't even ask him to find a higher-ranking officer for me, and I didn't think it was necessary to have any of those officers there at the time. They were all involved in various military operations, and as I have already explained, battles -- large-scale battles were ongoing in the Konjevic Polje area, and I never contacted them directly to ask them for favours or to issue orders to them. That was something that was excluded. That was not done. I apologise, but naturally I could have probably told that officer -- I could have asked him if he could find me Momir, if he could find Momir for me. But I don't know why I would have needed Momir Nikolic at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: No, the question is related to why you can say that it was impossible to find Nikolic those nights and then now you're not sure if he attended that discussion in your office or not.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. You mean how is it that I didn't inform him about that meeting? Is that what you are saying? I haven't understood the question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I don't understand your answers. That's a problem. You told us here that you were not sure that Nikolic attended this discussion in your office -- at your office on the 13th July in the evening, late evening. On the other side, I found in your statement that you were very sure that it was impossible to find Nikolic on those nights. So these are two absolutely contradicting questions -- answers. On the one hand, you are not sure if he was there; on the other side, you said it was impossible to find him. I want to know which one is the one that now is more near your memory, at least.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've understood your question, but help me a little more. If I said that I wasn't sure, that means that perhaps he was there, and that is what has given rise to doubt, because I previously excluded such a possibility. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to say why I said that I wasn't sure whether Momir had attended that meeting. I'll be quite specific. I'm not aware of any facts -- I'm not aware of a single reason for which such a thing would be impossible. For example, if I knew that on that day Mr. Momir Nikolic was absent and that he was in Belgrade on that day, if that was the case, I would now say that Momir Nikolic did not attend that meeting. Since this is a very delicate matter that is being discussed and unfortunately the event is a tragic one and many people -- various people were involved, I have to be as objective as possible. This is my responsibility. I allow for this possibility because I'm not aware of any facts that would make this impossible, and that is why I said that I allow for such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me there's no questions from the parties at this moment. Well, witness, thank you very much for giving your evidence. In my view, your appearance in this proceeding as a witness is sufficient to show your willingness to cooperate with this Tribunal. The usher will show you out of this room. I would like to thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I hope I have been of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, would you please tell your name, your date of birth, and the place to us.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mile Petrovic, born on the 25th of February, 1967 in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What is your present address now?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I live in the village of Bjelovac in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What was your position in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I mean did you ever serve in the army of the -- serve in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I started -- do you mean from the beginning to the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I started sometime in March in 1993 until 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What was your position in that brigade in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have any rank or positions?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you remember you made any statement to the Bratunac police station, to the Defence, or to anybody else concerning the incidents that happened in that period?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I gave a statement first in the police station and later on to an investigator. What was his name? Risto Dugonjic, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you remember the contents of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Tell us something about that statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, he asked me about the events in July 1995, about the encounter between Mr. Nikolic and me, what he said -- or rather, what he said here before the court, whether I had heard about that. I replied that I had heard about it and that I'd read about it in the papers. I think the newspaper was called Dnevni Avaz. He then asked me to tell him how these events had developed and taken place, and I told him that I was on my way home to the police station, and I ran into Mr. Momir Nikolic on the road, and he told me to go to the police station and wait for him there. That's what I did. I arrived at the station, and I asked the duty officer where the commander was, (redacted), in order to report to him, since he had allowed me to go home and visit my sick child. The duty officer told me he was in the park -- or rather, in the car park behind the building. I went there, and I found (redacted) there, and I reported to him. I said I'd come back, and I told him what Momir Nikolic had told me, that is, that I should come there and wait for him. After some time - I'm not sure whether it was half an hour or an hour - Momir Nikolic arrived and (redacted) to start the engine to have UN transporter -- personnel carrier and he told me we were going to Konjevic Polje, and this is what we did. So we set out towards Konjevic Polje, that is, Momir Nikolic, (redacted), and I. Momir Nikolic was where the commander usually stands. I was where the anti-aircraft gun was, and (redacted) was driving the personnel carrier. And so we proceeded in the direction of Konjevic Polje, and before we had arrived in Konjevic Polje, on the left-hand side of the road two civilians came out into the street, and Momir Nikolic told (redacted) to stop the vehicle, and he said, and he told me to get out and to search those two men and get them into the personnel carrier. I did this. When they had climbed into the personnel carrier, Momir Nikolic hit one of them on the head with a rifle, and then we continued on our way to Konjevic Polje. In Konjevic Polje, we stopped the vehicle and got out. Momir Nikolic took those two men and took them to the left side of the road, and there was a slab there, a slab, and he talked to them there. And when he had finished talking to them, he called me over and told me to take them to the building across the road. When I got there, there was some other soldiers there. I don't know what brigade they belonged to. So I started taking those men there, and the men who were standing there said I had nothing to do with them and I could leave. They said they would take the two men there with the others, because there were five or six other men there, and they were questioning them. Then I went back. In fact, Momir Nikolic had got out before that and he was talking to some foreigners. There were two foreigners in uniforms there, UN uniforms. And I passed by them. I heard them speaking English. And I was there near the personnel carrier with (redacted). Then Nikolic approached the personnel carrier and said that we should take these two soldiers wherever they wanted to go, and they got into the personnel carrier with us and we took them some 2 miles along the road towards Bratunac. Then they told us to go back, and we did, and the jeep came along and they got into the jeep, with the driver, and left. After a while - it may have been half an hour or an hour - we went back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in that armoured personnel carrier, did you use a megaphone or loudspeaker in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No. There wasn't a loudspeaker there, and I didn't use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you know the destination of those two surrendering Muslims at last?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were taken to that house. And you mean from there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were taken with the others, across the road to another building. It was a long building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When you came back to the vehicle, did you say anything to Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: To Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say anything. I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Were there any gunshots you heard at that place?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: There was shooting everywhere. You could hear gunfire all around. You could hear firing all around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from the Defence team? Mr. Londrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Londrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm attorney at law Veselin Londrovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Momir Nikolic, and I will put certain questions to you. Mr. Petrovic, can you tell Their Honours how many statements you made altogether, up to now, whether to the Bratunac police station, the investigator, or the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the Bratunac SUP, I made a statement. Then I made one to - what's his name - Dugonjic, the same statement. And I gave one to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never gave me a written statement.

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a written statement, but we did talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, when asked by His Honour, you replied that in July 1995 you worked as a military policeman. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any post in the Bratunac Brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, apart from the fact that I was told orally that I was a deputy of the commander. But I didn't feel like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, were you the deputy commander of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILE PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was not given a document. I was just told orally by Nikolic that I was to stand in for (redacted) when he wasn't around.
